TCP = statefull, UDP = stateless.

Simple version, not exactly correct but it works.

TCP Data (packets) have a order number, the way they are chopped up matters for their reassembly (Considered to be more reliable for obvious reasons). As such, for data that must be maintained and treated with care you would use TCP.

UDP, being stateless, you can lose data(packets) and it wont matter much for the overall end result. I.E. you can have data/packets lost and it wont matter (depending on how much).

Things like voice chat tend to be UDP because it is "lossy" and often can have missed packets without significant failures.

I.E. If it matters and you care about it. TCP. If you dont give a f**** and are just throwing things at the wall to see if it sticks.. UDP is probably ok.

This is another explination that is more verbose but explains it well.

https://nordvpn.com/blog/tcp-or-udp-which-is-better/

So in terms of practical use, using a voice chat service that uses TCP would be ideal for recording a podcast if you wanted to record it all from one person's machine rather than each person record separately and stitch it back together later. Is that me understanding this properly?

Not exactly. It really matters more about the type of data that you are working with. Voice/audio data tends to work well under UDP because by its nature does not need to be "perfect". Think about how audio sampling works with CD's or Radio.. You dont need "perfect reconstruction" for the audio to "sound right".

However, for data that needs to be "more perfect" (like using a VPN) you want something like TCP.. Partially because you want to be able to verify that your data is "exactly" what was requested and that it was not tampered with somehow.

TCP also tends to be more picky. If you "drop" (lose) a packet, your system will request the remote source to re-transmit that packet. UDP will just keep chugging along without a care (unless you lose too many packets). This also results in TCP being slower and more processor intensive while UDP is less accurate but faster (as long as loss is ok for your use).
